content.title: Artemis II rocket launch may be visible outside of Florida. See map
content.text: March 31, 2026Updated April 1, 2026, 4:41 p.m. ETFlorida rocket launches have been seen as far as Myrtle Beach, Georgia and New Jersey.What is Artemis II? 3 NASA astronauts and a Canadian astronaut will venture around the moon and back during a 10-day flight.Depending on weather and clouds, a Cape Canaveral rocket launch is sometimes visible in Jacksonville and West Palm Beach, Florida.Artemis II is a "go."All eyes are on NASA's massive Space Launch System rocket, which, after liftoff in Florida, may be spotted far beyond the launch pad.The space agency's SLS spacecraft is set to launch no earlier than 6:24 p.m. ET Wednesday, April 1, 2026, from Kennedy Space Center. This rocket launch near Cape Canaveral, Florida, will send four astronauts further in space than any humans before them.The second under NASA's multibillion-dollar moon program, the mission will send three Americans and one Canadian on a 10-day journey around the moon and back. While no landing is in store for the astronauts, the mission serves as a vital test flight to lay the groundwork for humans to make it back to the surface in as little as two years.Along the way, the Artemis II astronauts will make history, venturing about 250,000 miles in space – further than the record-setting Apollo 13 mission – and seeing a side of the moon that no human has ever seen.As of Tuesday, March 31, all signs are looking positive that the mission will get off the ground.Though rockets in Florida blast off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center or nearby Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, it's possible for spacecraft to be seen far beyond the launch pad, including in other states: In December 2023, the SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket was spotted from Boca Raton to Cedar Key to Myrtle Beach. And in February 2025, people in Fayetteville, North Carolina, posted photos and video of a Falcon 9 rocket after liftoff from Cape Canaveral, Florida. More recently, in February 2026, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket was seen about 150 miles away from Cape Canaveral in West Palm Beach, Florida.Pending weather conditions and cloud cover, the Artemis II mission's SLS rocket launch could be visible for most of Florida to parts of Georgia, according to NASA.In Florida, we can best see this moment in person, particularly if you're anywhere on the Space Coast (Melbourne, Florida, area), the Fun Coast (Daytona Beach area) or the Treasure Coast (Vero Beach, Jensen Beach and Fort Pierce).What time is the Artemis II rocket launch from Kennedy Space Center in Florida?NASA's Artemis II mission: 3 NASA astronauts and a Canadian astronaut will venture around the moon and back during a 10-day flight, helping pave the way for future crewed lunar exploration missions. Towering at 322 feet tall, the SLS rocket will generate 8.8 million pounds of thrust, making it the most powerful spacecraft NASA has ever launched.Launch: 6:24 p.m. ET Wednesday, April 1, 2026, with a two-hour windowLaunch trajectory: EastLaunch location: Launch Pad 39B at NASA's Kennedy Space Center near Cape Canaveral, FloridaSonic booms for the Space Coast of Florida: NoLive FLORIDA TODAY Space Team coverage: Starts hours before liftoff at floridatoday.com/space.The visibility map provided by NASA shows about when and where your best chances are to see the rocket as it streaks into space.The SLS rocket is composed of a 212-foot core stage propelled by four engines powered by a mix of liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, as well as two 177-feet-tall solid rocket boosters mounted to the sides providing the bulk of the thrust – a measure of the amount of force used to push the vehicle off the ground – and giving a great show to those watching.Which cities can see NASA Artemis II rocket launch from Kennedy Space Center in Florida?NASA provided a helpful graphic (see above) that shows the Atlas V rocket launch and its intended flight path and launch visibility. Note: Cities in the Space Coast of Florida, which is in Brevard County and measures 72 miles of coast, include Titusville, Mims, Port St. John, Merritt Island, Cocoa, Cocoa Beach, Melbourne, West Melbourne, Palm Bay, Satellite Beach, Indian Harbour Beach, Indialantic, Melbourne Beach, Grant-Valkaria and Sebastian.Launch, Florida's Space Coast1: Launch + 10 seconds, Space Coast, east Orlando2: Launch + 20 seconds, Space Coast, Orlando, near University of Central Florida, Bithlo, Kissimmee, the northern part of the Treasure Coast, Indian River County, Sebastian, Vero Beach, parts of Volusia County, Daytona Beach, New Smyrna Beach and Oak Hill3: Launch + 30 seconds, Space Coast, Orlando, Winter Park, the Treasure Coast, Indian River County, Sebastian, Vero Beach, Fort Pierce, Stuart, Port St. Lucie, Jensen Beach, Martin County, St. Lucie County, Daytona Beach, New Smyrna Beach, Oak Hill, Ormond Beach, Volusia County, Ocala, Lakeland area, Central Florida, Sanford, St. Augustine, Ponte Vedra Beach, near Jacksonville4: Launch + 40 seconds, visibility includes most of Florida, extending to Jacksonville, with these cities and counties in the visibility map: Sebring, Winter Haven, Palatka, Gainesville, Sarasota, Manatee County, Sarasota County, Cape Coral, Fort Myers, Naples, Collier County, Lee County, St. Petersburg, Tampa, Clearwater, Hillsborough County, Pinellas County, West Palm Beach, Lake Worth Beach, Wellington, Jupiter, Mar-a-Lago, Palm Beach, Palm Beach County5: Launch + 50 seconds, NASA Artemis II SLS rocket launch visibility extends across most of Florida to parts of Georgia, visibility still includes Florida, including Fernandina Beach, Lake City, West Palm Beach, Fort Myers, Naples, Fort Lauderdale, just outside Brunswick, Georgia, and Valdosta, Georgia6: Launch + 60 seconds, NASA SLS rocket launch visibility extends to the Big Bend area of Florida, near Tallahassee and Leon County, to Southern Georgia.7: Launch + 70 seconds, NASA SLS rocket launch visibility extends includes most of Florida up to Tallahassee and south past Miami to South Georgia. Visibility may include Savannah, Georgia.The above guidelines are estimates based on the graphic provided by NASA.Photos of NASA Artemis II SLS rocket at Kennedy Space Center in Florida Watch Artemis II rocket launch from Florida with NASA on Prime VideoNASA content, including some rocket launches and the highly anticipated Artemis II mission from Kennedy Space Center in Florida, is available to watch through NASA+ on desktop, both from its official site and YouTube. The platform is also available to download as a mobile app on smartphones.All NASA+ content is also available to those who have Prime Video downloaded on any of their devices – whether it be a smartphone or smart TV.Watch NASA+ content with Amazon Prime VideoThe content, which does not require a Prime subscription to view, is one of Prime Video's FAST channels (free ad-supported television).
